findings.text: The maximum protocol number follows the maximum address family number, so protocol table sizing tracks address family sizing. A separate socket state flag uses one high bit to record that listen has been performed.

The legacy socket multiplexor assigns sequential small integers starting at one for socket creation and ending at twenty for batched send, giving each of bind, connect, listen, accept, local and peer name lookup, pair creation, basic send and receive, directed send and receive, shutdown, option set and get, message send and receive, extended accept, and batched receive a distinct stable number in that interval.

A socket occupies one of five ordered lifecycle states with free meaning unallocated at zero, followed by unconnected, connecting while establishment is in progress, connected, and disconnecting while teardown is in progress.
Hardware timestamp provider quality uses a tiny ordered enumeration with precise first and approximate second, closed by a count marker, so only the two values below the count are valid qualifiers.

Timestamping options form a bitmask with distinct bits for transmit and receive in hardware and software, software fallback, system versus raw hardware time base, packet identifier attachment with a TCP-specific form, scheduler and acknowledgement and completion delivery, control message versus data-only versus statistics versus packet info reporting, combined transmit software-or-hardware indication, physical clock binding, and receive filtering. The completion bit is both the highest defined bit and the last marker, and the overall mask covers every bit through that marker.

The transmit record mask is the union of the transmit-side request bits covering hardware, software, scheduler, acknowledgement, and completion reporting, suitable for testing whether any transmit timestamp was asked for.
Timestamping configuration is two consecutive signed integers, the first for option flags and the second for the bound physical clock identifier, with no pointers or hidden fields shown.
Hardware timestamp configuration is three consecutive signed integers in order for general flags, transmit type selector, and receive filter selector.
Hardware timestamp flags presently define one low bit that requests the active bonded interface clock index, with last and mask helpers derived from that single bit so only that bit is valid.

The bonded clock index obtained through the bonding flag can change on failover when the active interface changes, so it must be treated as unstable, re-queried after topology changes, and never cached as a durable identifier.

Transmit timestamping moves from disabled through enabled with per-packet opt-in to one-step modes that also insert timestamps directly into synchronization packets or into both synchronization and peer-delay response packets. The one-step synchronization mode suppresses error-queue delivery for transmitted synchronization packets, and the peer-to-peer one-step mode suppresses it for both synchronization and peer-delay response packets, with a trailing count marking the end of selectors.

Receive filtering is an ordered selector from none through all and a some-superset indicator, then protocol-specific values for time protocol versions one and two over datagram and layer-two transports split by event versus synchronization versus delay-request coverage, plus transport-agnostic event, synchronization, and delay-request values and a catch-all network time value, closed by a count marker.

Packet timestamp ancillary data holds an interface index followed by packet length and two reserved words, all as fixed-width unsigned thirty-two-bit fields, with the trailing words reserved for future use.
Scheduled transmit flags define a low deadline-mode bit and a following error-reporting bit, with last and mask helpers derived from the second bit so only those two bits are currently valid.
Scheduled transmit settings pair a kernel clock identifier for the reference clock with an unsigned thirty-two-bit flags word interpreted under the scheduled transmit flag definitions.
The network device control family rendezvous uses the textual name netdev with numeric version one, fixing discovery for device, queue, page pool, and statistics operations.

Data-path acceleration capabilities are powers of two for basic operation, redirect, native transmit, zero-copy, hardware offload, receive scatter-gather, and native transmit scatter-gather, with a private mask covering all seven bits.
Receive metadata capabilities use separate low bits to advertise timestamp, hash, and virtual network tag availability.

Zero-copy device flags use separate low bits for transmit timestamp, transmit checksum, and launch-time queueing discipline. Queue direction has two values for receive versus transmit, queue statistics scope presently defines a single queue value of one, and threading control has three states for disabled, enabled, and busy-poll operation.

Device, page pool, NAPI, and queue objects each use independent one-based attribute namespaces closed by private maxima with public maxima one less. Device attributes number one through six, page pool and NAPI and queue attributes each number one through eight, covering interface, queue, and NAPI identity, feature words, memory and binding handles, interrupt and process identity, deferral and timeout tuning, and threading state. A provider-info namespace carries a single receive buffer length, and the zero-copy info namespace is currently empty apart from its maximum markers.

Pool and queue statistics reserve low identifiers for addressing and begin counters at eight with gaps left unused. Pool info uses identifier one while pool counters run eight through eighteen distinguishing fast and slow and empty allocation paths with high-order, refill, waive, and cached versus ring recycling outcomes including full and refcount-released cases. Queue addressing uses one through four while queue counters run eight through thirty-four separating receive and transmit packets and bytes plus allocation failure, hardware drops with overruns and rate limits, checksum outcomes, hardware aggregation wire versus aggregated accounting, and transmit stop versus wake signals.

The control protocol exposes sequential commands numbered one through sixteen for device, page pool, queue, NAPI, and statistics retrieval with add, delete, and change notifications plus receive and transmit binding, NAPI setting, and queue creation, delimited by private and public maxima. Lease attributes carry interface, queue, and namespace identity, buffer attributes carry interface, queue list, file descriptor, identifier, and page size, and two multicast groups named mgmt and page-pool distribute management and pool events.
The largest hardware address occupies thirty-two bytes, bounding link-layer storage, and the initial device group identifier is zero.
Name origin uses zero for unknown kernel-internal, one for kernel enumeration, two for predictable kernel naming, three for user-space provision, and four for user-space rename.
Wired port types form a zero-based sequence for unknown, two ten-megabit copper forms, attachment unit interface, and three hundred-megabit forms split by twisted-pair versus fiber encodings.
Address provenance uses zero for permanent default, one for random generation, two for reuse from another device, and three for assignment through the device address setter.

Filter verdicts are consecutive integers from zero for drop through accept, stolen, queue, repeat, and stop, with the maximum verdict equated to stop and stop retained only for user-space queue compatibility.

The low eight bits hold the verdict, one middle bit requests queue bypass, and the high sixteen bits hold auxiliary data with sixteen giving both shift and width. Queue selection shifts the queue number into the high half and combines it with the queue verdict, while errored drop negates the error code, shifts it into the high half, and combines it with the drop verdict.

Internet hooks run in fixed order from pre-routing through local input, forward, local output, and post-routing with a count marker, and ingress is aliased to that count rather than extending the classic range. Device hooks define ingress, egress, and a count. Family selectors are sparse with zero for unspecified, one for internet, two for version four, three for address resolution, five for net device, seven for bridge, and ten for version six, followed by a count.
Network address storage is a union overlaying raw words with big-endian version-four and version-six views and system address structure views, so the same bytes can serve either family.

Tracking state combines a base of established, related, or new with a reply offset added for the return path, giving derived established-reply and related-reply values and no new value in the reply direction, plus a distinct count marker and a separate untracked value whose numeric position differs between kernel and user-space views.
State mask bits place invalid at bit zero, derive established, related, and new bits by folding the base value modulo the reply offset, and place untracked at bit six.

Status flags occupy successive bits zero through fifteen in lifecycle order from expected through reply-seen, assured, confirmed, source and destination translation needs, sequence adjustment, source and destination completion, dying, fixed timeout, template, obsolete untracked, helper, flow offload, and hardware offload, with combined masks for translation needs and completions and an unchangeable mask shielding translation, confirmation, dying, adjustment, template, offload, and obsolete bits from direct user writes.

The bit long reserved for obsolete untracked entries is repurposed in kernel builds to mark insertion collisions, so the same numeric bit means different things inside and outside the kernel. Expected and translation-need flags never change, reply-seen and assured and dying flags can only be set, and dying entries are already detached from lookup lists.

Tracking events enumerate creation, related creation, destruction, first bidirectional traffic, promotion to assured, protocol info change, helper assignment, mark and security mark changes, sequence adjustment change with an alias for translation sequence adjustment, label change, and proxy change, closed by a kernel-only maximum. Expectation events define only creation and destruction.
Expectation flags use successive low bits starting at zero for permanent, inactive, user-space ownership, and dead state, while the public mask covers only the first three and excludes dead.
Tuple direction uses zero for original, one for reply, and two as the maximum marker.

Manipulable transport fields share a sixteen-bit big-endian overlay with per-protocol views for stream, datagram, congestion-controlled, and datagram-congestion ports, control-message identifier, and routing-encapsulation key where only sixteen bits of the wider thirty-two-bit key are used for the point-to-point tunneling use.
Direction is derived by comparing tracking info against the reply threshold, yielding reply at or above the threshold and original below it.
Generic, table, chain, set, and object names each allow up to two hundred fifty-six bytes, user data allows up to two hundred fifty-six bytes, and fingerprint genre strings allow up to sixteen bytes.

The register file offers a dedicated verdict register plus four data registers, followed by sixteen thirty-two-bit lanes numbered zero through fifteen beginning at offset eight, with public maxima marking the last data register and the last thirty-two-bit lane.
Each full register spans sixteen bytes and each thirty-two-bit lane spans four bytes, with the lane count defined as the inclusive span from the first to the last lane.
Control verdicts use negative integers minus one through minus five for continue, break, jump, goto, and return, keeping them disjoint from the non-negative filter verdict range.
Each user-space header carries a unique inclusion guard so repeated inclusion yields one definition set, with no runtime behavior attached to the guards.
